To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the amplitude of rodent cycles is related to vegetation properties in tundras.
the strength and direction of the relationships between rodents and their food and shelter plants are temporally and spatially variable.

the strength of plant-rodent interactions is spatially consistent but temporally inconsistent, and that this temporal inconsistency limits the ability to predict rodent abundance from plant properties.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the spatial and temporal transferability of plant-rodent interactions.
understanding the consequences of variability in biotic interactions for the functioning of food webs.

the transferability of biotically mediated processes across time and space, and we argue that the transferability of models is likely to increase with a deeper mechanistic understanding of food web processes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the transferability of biotically based models of population dynamics in tundra ecosystems is poor.
the spatial transferability of rodent plant relationships is good and that the temporal transferability is poor.
the temporal transferability and predictability of plant-rodent relationships is poor.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
biotic interactions in food webs are complex and that we need to better understand the consequences of the variability in these interactions for predicting population dynamics.
the transferability of biogeographical models is likely to improve with a better understanding of the variability of biotic interaction strength.
we need to understand the variability of biotic interaction strength in order to predict species abundance and distribution in a changing climate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the transferability of biotically driven population dynamics models is poor and that the consequences of this for predicting population dynamics and species distribution are unknown.
we need to improve our ability to predict species distribution, population dynamics and ecosystem functioning in a world that is rapidly changing.
the temporal variability of biogeography and food webs should be taken into account in the development of ecological theory and in management of species of interest.
